lead: The z-transform turns a sequence x[n] into a function X(z) of a complex variable z. It exists because the DTFT does not converge for every sequence. Adding the real factor r = |z| lets the sum converge in a ring of the z-plane. That ring, the region of convergence or ROC, is part of the answer. Without it, the algebra cannot tell a right-sided sequence from a left-sided one. Engineers use this in difference-equation solving, digital filter design, control, and any place where a sampled signal needs a compact frequency-domain description.
prereq: You need: Unit 4 (Laplace transform and ROC) and the DTFT definition in chapter 6.2.

blocks.where: x[n] is the sequence; z is a complex number; n is an integer index.

blocks.text: Write z = r e<sup>jθ</sup>, where r = |z| is the radius and θ is the angle. The magnitude of a term is |x[n]| r<sup>−n</sup>, because |z<sup>−n</sup>| = r<sup>−n</sup>. The series converges absolutely when Σ |x[n]| r<sup>−n</sup> < ∞. The ROC is the set of all z for which this inequality holds. Absolute convergence is stronger than ordinary convergence, and it is the standard definition here.
If z = ejω, then r = 1 and X(ejω) = Σ x[n] e−jωn, the DTFT of chapter 6.2. This equality holds only when the unit circle |z| = 1 lies inside the ROC.

Convergence depends on r, not on θ. So the ROC is built from circles centred at z = 0. It is a ring (an annulus), the outside of one circle, the inside of one circle, or the whole plane with possible holes at 0 or ∞. It is connected, and it contains no poles of X(z). A pole is a value of z where X(z) becomes infinite; absolute convergence cannot hold there.

Four cases cover most exam questions. A finite-length sequence is nonzero only for n<sub>1</sub> ≤ n ≤ n<sub>2</sub>. Its ROC is the whole z-plane except possibly z = 0 (when n<sub>2</sub> > 0) and z = ∞ (when n<sub>1</sub> < 0). A right-sided sequence is zero for n < N<sub>0</sub>; its ROC is |z| > r<sub>2</sub>, outside the outermost pole radius. A left-sided sequence is zero for n > N<sub>0</sub>; its ROC is |z| < r<sub>1</sub>, inside the innermost pole radius. A two-sided sequence has an annulus r<sub>2</sub> < |z| < r<sub>1</sub>. If the two inequalities do not overlap, the z-transform does not exist.

The unit circle is the set |z| = 1. If it lies inside the ROC, the DTFT exists and equals X(e<sup>jω</sup>). If it does not, the DTFT does not exist as an ordinary function, even though the z-transform algebra may look finite.

sections.h3: Standard pairs and the pole-zero plot

items: δ[n] ↔ 1 for all z. The unit impulse has no pole.
u[n] ↔ z/(z − 1) for |z| > 1. The pole is at z = 1.
a<sup>n</sup>u[n] ↔ z/(z − a) for |z| > |a|. This is right-sided.
−a<sup>n</sup>u[−n − 1] ↔ z/(z − a) for |z| < |a|. This is left-sided.

blocks.text: For a = 1/3, both sequences give z/(z − 1/3), but the right-sided one has ROC |z| > 1/3 and the left-sided one has ROC |z| < 1/3. In a pole-zero plot, poles are marked × and zeros ○. The ROC is a region that stops at poles; it never crosses one. The mapping z = e<sup>sT</sup> connects this picture to Unit 4. Here s = σ + jω is the Laplace variable and T is the sampling interval. The left half of the s-plane, σ < 0, maps to |z| < 1 inside the unit circle; σ = 0 maps to |z| = 1.

figure.caption: For (1/3)<sup>n</sup>u[n], the dashed radius ends at the pole 1/3. The ROC is outside that pole circle; the solid unit circle lies inside the ROC, so the DTFT exists.

spec.aria: A point at the origin, a dashed radius to the pole at one third, and a solid radius to the unit circle at one.

examples.question: Find X(z), the poles, the zeros and the ROC for x[n] = (1/3)<sup>n</sup>u[n] − (1/2)<sup>n</sup>u[−n − 1]. State whether the DTFT exists.
steps: First term: set a = 1/3. The pair a<sup>n</sup>u[n] ↔ z/(z − a) gives X<sub>1</sub>(z) = z/(z − 1/3), ROC |z| > 1/3.
Second term: set a = 1/2. The pair −a<sup>n</sup>u[−n − 1] ↔ z/(z − a) with ROC |z| < |a| gives X<sub>2</sub>(z) = z/(z − 1/2), ROC |z| < 1/2.
Poles solve z − 1/3 = 0 and z − 1/2 = 0: z = 1/3 and z = 1/2. Zeros solve z = 0 and 2z − 5/6 = 0: z = 0 and z = 5/12 ≈ 0.4167.
ROC is the overlap |z| > 1/3 and |z| < 1/2, so 1/3 < |z| < 1/2.
The unit circle has |z| = 1. It is not in the ROC because 1 > 1/2. Therefore the DTFT does not exist.
examples.answer: X(z) = z(2z − 5/6)/[(z − 1/3)(z − 1/2)], poles at z = 1/3 and z = 1/2, zeros at z = 0 and z = 5/12, ROC 1/3 < |z| < 1/2; no DTFT exists.
examples.check:
p1 = 1/3
p2 = 1/2
z0 = 5/12
unit = 1.0
print(f'{p1:.16g}')
print(f'{p2:.16g}')
print(f'{z0:.16g}')
print(f'{unit:.1f}')

traps: Two different sequences share the same X(z). The pair a<sup>n</sup>u[n] and −a<sup>n</sup>u[−n−1] both give z/(z−a). An answer with no ROC is incomplete.
A pole can sit at z = 0 or z = ∞ after a shift. For δ[n−1], X(z) = z<sup>−1</sup>, so z = 0 is excluded even though the sequence is finite length.
The ROC never includes a pole. If your region contains z = 1/3 or z = 1/2 in the worked example, it is wrong.
The unit circle test is not optional. If |z| = 1 is outside the ROC, do not write X(e<sup>jω</sup>); say the DTFT does not exist.
Right-sided gives |z| > r<sub>2</sub> and left-sided gives |z| < r<sub>1</sub>; do not swap the inequalities. A two-sided sequence needs an annulus, not a half-plane.

quiz.a: The set of z for which Σ |x[n] z<sup>−n</sup>| is finite.

quiz.q: Why can no pole lie inside the ROC?
quiz.a: At a pole X(z) is infinite, so absolute convergence fails; the defining sum cannot be finite there.

quiz.q: For x[n] = (1/4)<sup>n</sup>u[n], find X(z), the pole, the ROC, and state whether the DTFT exists.
quiz.a: X(z) = z/(z − 1/4), pole at z = 1/4, ROC |z| > 1/4. The unit circle |z| = 1 is inside, so the DTFT exists.

quiz.q: Two sequences have X(z) = z/(z − 0.8). One is right-sided and one is left-sided. Which can have a DTFT?
quiz.a: Right-sided has ROC |z| > 0.8, which contains |z| = 1. Left-sided has ROC |z| < 0.8, which does not. Only the right-sided sequence has a DTFT.

quiz.q: Find the ROC for x[n] = 2<sup>n</sup>u[n] − 3<sup>n</sup>u[−n − 1], and state whether the DTFT exists.
quiz.a: First term ROC |z| > 2. Second term ROC |z| < 3. Overlap is 2 < |z| < 3. The unit circle |z| = 1 is outside, so no DTFT.

quiz.q: If the unit circle lies in the ROC, what is X(e<sup>jω</sup>)?
quiz.a: It is the DTFT of x[n], equal to X(z) evaluated at z = e<sup>jω</sup>.

beyond: Not for the exam. The z-transform is the workhorse of digital control and DSP because it turns delays into multiplication by z<sup>−1</sup>. Modern software uses polynomial root finding and fast algorithms to move between sequences and z-domain models. The chirp z-transform evaluates X(z) on arcs other than the unit circle, useful in spectral zooming. Search next for chirp z-transform, cepstrum, and z-domain stability tests.
